title: What can we learn by making an everyday object work differently?
statement: Choose an object you use without thinking, like a drawer or a phone. Change how it works and see what you notice when you have to slow down and figure it out.

title: What makes a place feel like home?
statement: Think of one small thing somebody does that makes you feel like you belong there.

title: What do you notice after the rain?
statement: Go somewhere familiar just after a storm. Look down, listen, and share one thing you usually miss.

title: A Nightstand Held Together with Rubber Bands
statement: This nightstand is made from wood, rattan cane webbing, and rubber bands that resist the pull of the drawers. I cut the nightstand in half to show what happens inside. This was the first piece in my investigation, and it got me thinking about how a familiar object can make you notice the movement you usually take for granted.
alt: Two views of a wooden nightstand with partly open drawers held by rubber bands.
galleryCredit: Original sculpture from the artist’s AP 3-D Art and Design portfolio

title: A Phone Call You Have to Work For
statement: I took the idea from the nightstand and applied it to answering a phone. To take the call, you lift a rock from an antique chest and solve a small puzzle box. I wanted to see how far you could stretch an everyday interaction and how the extra steps could make it feel like a game.
alt: A large rock on an open wooden chest, with a puzzle box and cords on the ground.
galleryCredit: Original sculpture from the artist’s AP 3-D Art and Design portfolio

title: Gears Engraved with Spirograph Patterns
statement: I designed the gears in CAD and engraved spirograph patterns into the acrylic. The patterns made some of the gears harder to turn. Like the phone piece, this let me experiment with the tradeoff between how a mechanism looks and how easily it works. You can see the patterns and the gears together in the shallow birch case.
alt: Two views of blue and dark acrylic gears in a shallow plywood case.
galleryCredit: Original sculpture from the artist’s AP 3-D Art and Design portfolio

title: Trying to Answer in Time
statement: This sample poem imagines a friend calling while someone tries to figure out the rock and puzzle box in “A Phone Call You Have to Work For.”
text:
By the time I lift the rock,
you’ve called twice.

The little box opens sideways.
I figure it out
just as the ringing stops.

When I call you back,
I leave the rock on the floor.
You ask why I’m laughing.
I tell you to come try it.

title: Two Slices
statement: One slice for the person who woke up first. One for whoever comes down next. A little proof that somebody thought of you.
alt: Gouache-style painting of two slices of jam toast and mismatched mugs on a blue kitchen table.

title: Leave the Plate Out
statement: A poem for the second plate in “Two Slices,” told by the person who comes home late.
text:
The house is asleep.
I know which stair to skip.

On the blue table,
under a plate turned upside down,
one piece of toast.

The jam has gone dark at the edges.
I eat it standing there
before I take my coat off.

title: Kitchen Light
statement: Soft keys and a brushed rhythm turn the kitchen in “Two Slices” into a little instrumental. The tune leaves a gap, like the empty chair.

title: The Last Bus
statement: After the storm, an ordinary bus stop gets a second light: the one under your feet. The shelter glows in the puddle before a bus turns the corner.
alt: A warm bus shelter and its reflection in a puddle on a blue evening.

title: My Phone Says Two Minutes
statement: The person missing from “The Last Bus” gets a voice. The second plate in “Leave the Plate Out” gives them somewhere to go.
text:
Two minutes, says the app.
It has said that for ten.

The shelter drips on my left shoe.
A car puts red in the puddle
and takes it away.

Across town there’s toast
under a plate.
I can almost hear the plate
slide over the table.

title: Two More Minutes
statement: A pulse in pairs borrows the drip in the poem and the staggered lights in the image. A low note comes in near the end like a bus pulling up.

title: A Sculpture Made from a Keyboard
statement: I took apart a keyboard and rearranged its pieces into a sculpture, keeping the cords and lights visible. The nightstand still invites you to try its drawers. This piece goes further by giving the parts a new job altogether. It let me look at the shapes and textures of something I usually only think of as a tool.
alt: Two views of a dismantled keyboard reassembled into an illuminated sculpture.
galleryCredit: Original sculpture from the artist’s AP 3-D Art and Design portfolio

title: A Tower with Its Mechanism on Display
statement: I designed a working tower that could extend, then cut it open to expose the way it moved and rebuilt it as a sculpture. The fishing line stays visible against the blue structure, alongside mud and dried foliage. Like the engraved gears, it gives you a reason to look closely at parts that are usually hidden.
alt: A blue extending mechanism with exposed cable, set next to a rough block with dried foliage.
galleryCredit: Original sculpture from the artist’s AP 3-D Art and Design portfolio

title: A Launcher Rebuilt as a Sculpture
statement: This started as a working launcher. I gradually removed the parts it needed to launch anything, while keeping details such as the blue wheels, wood, and steel cable. The tower opened up a mechanism so people could see it. Here I wanted to see how much of the original object you could still recognize after its purpose changed.
alt: Three views of a small blue and wood mechanical sculpture with cable and wheels.
galleryCredit: Original sculpture from the artist’s AP 3-D Art and Design portfolio

title: Last Stop, Ten Seconds
statement: A ten-second moving study made from “The Last Bus” and “Two More Minutes.” The camera moves toward the puddle while the rhythm makes the empty stop feel like it’s waiting.
galleryCredit: AI-generated image and music, edited into a short film
